definition: The hottest, most sultry period of summer, traditionally reckoned as the roughly forty days when Sirius, the Dog Star, rises and sets with the sun; by extension, any period of stagnation or oppressive heat.
etymology: From Latin dies caniculares, the days of the little dog — Sirius belonging to Canis Major, the Great Dog. Ancient Romans believed the star's heliacal rising in late July added its heat to the sun's, cooking the air and making men listless and dogs mad. The phrase passed through medieval Latin into English by the sixteenth century, already carrying the sense of torpor as much as temperature.
usage: The office fans hummed without conviction; it was the dog-days, and even ambition had gone slack.
